meta.title: Who really said "Three generations from shirtsleeves to shirtsleeves"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Andrew Carnegie gets the credit, but the saying was in print by June 1874 and called "an old saying" in 1882 — and Oxford notes it is not found in his writings.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Three generations from shirtsleeves to shirtsleeves'?
meta.ogDescription: In print by June 1874, already "an old saying" by 1882, and absent from Carnegie's writings — an anonymous American proverb, not a Carnegie epigram.

answer.label: Not Andrew Carnegie — an anonymous American proverb
answer.authorDates: In print by June 1874 · called ‘an old saying’ by 1882
answer.sourceLine: Andrew Carnegie did not coin this. The saying was already in print — inside quotation marks, as something Americans were understood to say — in Appletons’ Journal of 27 June 1874, and by June 1882 The Atlantic Monthly introduced it as “an old saying.” The Oxford Dictionary of Phrase and Fable records that it is often attributed to Carnegie “but is not found in his writings.”

source.heading: Where the line actually comes from

docMeta.dd: Unknown — quoted as existing folk wisdom, not coined
Appletons’ Journal of Literature, Science, and Art, 27 June 1874, p. 802
Not present — the word ‘shirt-sleeves’ appears nowhere in Wealth (1889)

source.excerpt: Turn a university-man into the world of England, where every place is marked ‘taken,’ and what a hapless future awaits him!… In America, where there are “but three generations from shirt-sleeves to shirt-sleeves,” the whole of a son’s fortune is well spent upon his training, though he must go out into life with the tastes of a gentleman, and no income to sustain them.
trail: Appletons’ Journal of 27 June 1874, page 802, quotes it as settled American wisdom: “In America, where there are ‘but three generations from shirt-sleeves to shirt-sleeves,’ the whole of a son’s fortune is well spent upon his training.” We read the scanned issue.

Eight years later the economist Edward Atkinson opened a paragraph of “The Rapid Progress of Communism” with “It is an old saying that ‘it usually takes but three generations from shirt-sleeves to shirt-sleeves’” — The Atlantic Monthly, June 1882, p. 834.

Carnegie’s documented view of inherited money is close in spirit but different in words: in ‘Wealth,’ North American Review, June 1889, he writes that the thoughtful man must say “I would as soon leave to my son a curse as the almighty dollar.” The word ‘shirt-sleeves’ does not occur in that text.

The Oxford Dictionary of Phrase and Fable calls it a proverbial saying of the early 20th century — the 1874 and 1882 printings above push it back earlier — and states plainly that it is “often attributed to… Andrew Carnegie… but is not found in his writings.”
source.excerptNote: From an appreciation of the essayist Charles Dudley Warner in Appletons’ Journal, 27 June 1874, p. 802; word histories attributes the piece to the poet and critic Edmund Clarence Stedman. Note the quotation marks: the writer is repeating a saying already in circulation, not minting one.

source.rightsNote: The saying is an anonymous proverb with no author of record, and the earliest printings we could verify — Appletons’ Journal (27 June 1874) and The Atlantic Monthly (June 1882) — are periodicals long in the public domain in the United States. Nothing here is anyone’s protected property; the wording was common currency before either magazine set it in type.

author.name: Andrew Carnegie
author.heading: About Andrew Carnegie
author.bio: Born in Dunfermline, Scotland, Carnegie emigrated to Pennsylvania as a boy, built the largest steel business in the United States, and then spent the rest of his life giving the proceeds away — most famously to public libraries. He was also the era’s most quotable critic of inherited fortunes: in his 1889 essay Wealth he wrote that the thoughtful man must say “I would as soon leave to my son a curse as the almighty dollar.” That documented position is why the shirtsleeves proverb drifted onto his name — but the proverb was circulating in American print before he published a word about wealth.

cite.sourceCitation: “Charles Dudley Warner,” Appletons’ Journal of Literature, Science, and Art 11, no. 275 (June 27, 1874): 802; quoted again as “an old saying” in Edward Atkinson, “The Rapid Progress of Communism,” The Atlantic Monthly 49, no. 296 (June 1882): 834. No source in the writings of Andrew Carnegie.

misattribution.heading: Why Carnegie gets the credit
misattribution.intro: The line travels as a Carnegie epigram — on quote sites, in wealth-management brochures, on family-business conference slides. The paper trail does not support it.

items.why: Carnegie is the name almost always attached, yet nobody produces a speech, letter or book in which he says it. Wikiquote files the line under ‘Undated’, and its only citation is a 2001 economics book, George J. Borjas’s Heaven’s Door — a modern author repeating the proverb, not Carnegie writing it.

The tidy five-word epigram is a modern compression. The nineteenth-century printings are full sentences framed as folk wisdom, with the noun hyphenated: “it usually takes but three generations from shirt-sleeves to shirt-sleeves” (The Atlantic Monthly, June 1882).

items.who: ‘A Lancashire proverb Carnegie carried to America’
items.why: England has its own version — ‘from clogs to clogs in three generations,’ recorded in Lancashire papers in 1868 — and the two sayings are usually treated as counterparts. No source shows the Scottish-born Carnegie carrying either one across the Atlantic.

misattribution.truthLine: The honest answer: an anonymous American proverb, in print by 27 June 1874 and described as old by 1882. Nobody knows who said it first, and no evidence points to Carnegie.

context.heading: Why it mattered
lead: The proverb compresses a whole theory of family fortune into six words: the grandfather builds it in his working clothes, the son enjoys it, the grandson loses it and goes back to work. It is the standard epigraph of the family-wealth advisory trade, which is precisely why it wants a famous author — a proverb sounds like folklore, but a Carnegie line sounds like evidence.

Carnegie is the natural magnet because he was the era’s loudest voice on the moral peril of inherited money. His 1889 essay ‘Wealth,’ published in the North American Review, argues that great fortunes should not be left to children at all. But that essay appeared fifteen years after the saying was already being quoted in American magazines, and it never uses the phrase.
detailsBody: The 1874 appearance is not an economic argument at all — it sits inside a literary portrait of the essayist Charles Dudley Warner, where the writer uses the saying as an accepted fact about American life to explain why an American father should spend everything on his son’s education rather than hoard it for him.

By 1882 the economist Edward Atkinson was deploying the same phrase to make a policy point in The Atlantic Monthly: that American wealth disperses on its own, so communism had little to gain against it. Neither writer credits anyone. Both treat the words as public property — which is what a proverb is.
context.pull: It is an old saying that ‘it usually takes but three generations from shirt-sleeves to shirt-sleeves.’
